<h1>How it works</h1>
<p class="sub">One engine, in your browser, on files that stay where they are. What runs where, what is kept, what is checked.</p>

<h2>One engine</h2>
<p>diff-ref-struct is a Rietveld refinement project for the Mac: a core in Rust (the engine, with the command line <code>drs</code>), an app around it, and modules. The page runs the core's plotting part compiled to WebAssembly with <code>wasm-bindgen</code>, and the app's Plots module unchanged. The module asks the core with the same commands, names and data as in the Mac app; in the page a dispatcher answers them from the WebAssembly package instead of the app's process. So there is no second implementation of anything: a map, a step, a temperature read from a name is what the Mac app and <code>drs</code> give.</p>
<p>The browser does two things besides drawing: it reads files and saves downloads. Every calculation is the core's, including the ones that look small (a colour range, a stack's step, the rows' edges on a map).</p>

<h2>Checked, not assumed</h2>
<ul>
<li><b>The same numbers as the command line.</b> A test runs the WebAssembly core under Node on the Tb<sub>2</sub>Pd<sub>2</sub>Sn files, given by name and text as the browser gives them, and requires its map to equal <code>drs plots map --json</code>'s to the bit.</li>
<li><b>The same commands as the app.</b> A test requires the package to serve the commands the app's Plots module uses, by name.</li>
<li><b>Real runs.</b> The ESRF in-situ run of 101 scans (112&nbsp;MB) is the test of the series detector: its three sets found scan for scan as they had been built by hand, the exposure classes told apart.</li>
<li><b>The page's own parts</b> (the file tree, the address, live mode's reading, the offline list) are tested under Node on every publication; the publication stops if a test fails.</li>
</ul>

<h2>Your files</h2>
<ul>
<li><b>Read where they are.</b> Open Folder… gives the page a handle to read the folder (Chrome, Edge, Arc) or a list of its files (Firefox, Safari). A file's text is read when the core needs it, then handed to the core inside the page. Files over 64&nbsp;MB are not read.</li>
<li><b>Never sent.</b> The page has no server to send to: it is a set of static files. It loads its own files from its own address and nothing from elsewhere (no web fonts, no scripts from other sites, no counters).</li>
<li><b>Never written.</b> The page asks only to read. What you save (a <code>.drv</code>, a viewer page) is downloaded to your Downloads folder.</li>
<li><b>Kept in your browser.</b> The page's address keeps the view (names and numbers on screen, never content); local storage keeps your choices of theme, inspector width, tree order and live mode. Clear the site's data in the browser to forget them.</li>
</ul>

<h2>Offline</h2>
<p>A service worker keeps the page's own files: the list of every file the page loads (36 files, 4.4&nbsp;MB with the core) is written by a tool that walks the page's links and imports, and a test fails when it is not the page's. It never keeps a data file and never fetches one. A new version installs beside the old and replaces it; a tab open on the old one keeps it until reloaded.</p>

<h2>Published</h2>
<p>The page and this site are built by one GitHub Action from the project's repository on every change: the core compiled to WebAssembly, the tests run, the files staged, this site rendered with Quarto, a guard run against any trace of a team's unpublished data, all pushed to the public repository <code>diff-ref-struct-web</code> (branch <code>gh-pages</code>), served by GitHub Pages. The page is at the root, this site at <code>/guide/</code>. The source the page is built from goes to the same repository's <code>main</code> at each release, by a second Action, under the Apache License 2.0; the documents under CC BY 4.0.</p>

<p class="sub">See also: <a href="formats/index.html">the file formats</a>, <a href="../releases/index.html">the releases</a>, <a href="../conventions/index.html">the conventions</a>.</p>
